meta.title: The Kids Who Hacked the World, Part 1: The 17-Year-Old Who Hacked Twitter
meta.working_title: The 17-Year-Old Who Hacked Obama's Twitter (The Kids Who Hacked the World, Part 1)
meta.device: A 'blue bird' wall of famous accounts that light up red one by one as they fall, with a running count and a crypto wallet meter that fills with each scam tweet. Each phase of the hack opens with a big PHASE 1 / 2 / 3 card.
meta.style: Internet-crime caper in the house 2D style, Gumball/t-shirt character style (as in NVIDIA). Painted plates: a teenager's dark bedroom with RGB lights in Tampa, a Minecraft-ish blocky game world, a shady forum on a giant screen, a phone-shop counter, Twitter's open-plan office at night, a crisis room with red alerts, a courtroom on a video call. Neon blue, purple and alert red. Famous people never drawn: only their names on tweet cards. Methods kept high level (no how-to). SFX under the VO (keyboard clicks, Discord pings, phone rings, alarm beeps), music only at combine.
meta.source: English compilation transcript 'The Kids Who Hacked the World', segment 4 (~3,200 words), fully rewritten. Sponsor read and archive clips cut. Court-record facts only; methods kept high level.

shots.vo: A Twitter employee gets a phone call from the company's help desk. There's a problem with his work login. Could he sign in again, please?
shots.visual: An employee at a desk answers a phone; a friendly voice bubble.

shots.vo: He does. The caller thanks him and hangs up. He isn't the help desk. He's a 17-year-old in Florida with a jewelled Rolex.
shots.visual: The caller's side: a dark bedroom, a teenager grinning at a screen.
shots.anim: He hangs up and spins in his chair.

shots.vo: Within a day he takes over the Twitter accounts of Obama, Biden, Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk, and uses them to run a Bitcoin scam.
shots.visual: A wall of famous account cards flips red one by one.
shots.anim: Cards flip red in a wave.

shots.visual: Title over the red wall.
shots.onscreen: THE KIDS WHO HACKED THE WORLD · PART 1

shots.vo: 2016, Tampa, Florida. Graham Ivan Clark is 13, home-schooled, and plays Minecraft for hours. His parents split up when he was seven.
shots.visual: A bedroom with a blocky game on screen; a boy at the desk.

shots.vo: Online he sells rare game items and cool usernames. The catch: buyers often never get them. Other players make videos calling him a scammer.
shots.visual: A shop sign 'RARE SKINS' on screen; angry chat bubbles pile up.
shots.anim: Coins drop in; angry bubbles stack.

shots.vo: By his own account, at 14 he's making about 5,000 dollars a month.
shots.visual: A tiny stack of cash growing next to the keyboard.

shots.vo: Then he finds OGUsers, a shady forum where people trade stolen accounts and rare usernames. He's banned within days, for taking money and not delivering.
shots.visual: A dark forum page on a giant screen; a red BANNED stamp.

shots.vo: On the forum he learns about a scam called SIM swapping. Criminals trick a phone company into moving your number to their SIM card.
shots.visual: A phone-shop counter; a stranger hands over a fake ID; a SIM card changes hands.

shots.vo: Many accounts send login codes by text. So whoever controls your number can reset your passwords, from email to bank to crypto.
shots.visual: A phone with a padlock; arrows to email, bank and crypto icons; locks pop open.
shots.anim: Locks pop open one by one.

shots.vo: In 2019 a Seattle investor, Greg Bennett, lost over 100 Bitcoin this way. The New York Times later linked the attack to Graham's online alias. He was a minor, and was never charged for it.
shots.visual: A man staring at a dead phone; his crypto wallet emptying.
shots.anim: Phone shows NO SIGNAL; wallet drains.

shots.vo: Soon afterwards, Graham is living large: his own apartment, a white BMW, a Rolex covered in gems. He's still 17.
shots.visual: A teen leaning on a white car, flashing a sparkly watch.

shots.vo: July 2020. His new plan: forget hacking stars one by one. Get inside Twitter itself, and take any account he wants.
shots.visual: A PHASE 1 card; a map of Twitter's office with a red target.

shots.vo: He tells a few people online that he works at Twitter. A small crew forms on Discord.
shots.visual: A chat window filling with usernames joining.

shots.vo: Using LinkedIn, he finds Twitter employees and phones them, pretending to be the internal help desk. Most hang up. A few report him.
shots.visual: A wall of employee profile cards; most with a hang-up icon.
shots.anim: Cards flip: hang up, hang up, report.

shots.vo: But one employee believes him, and signs in on a fake login page. Graham uses those details, and the code from the employee's phone, to get onto Twitter's network.
shots.visual: A real login page next to a fake twin; a key copies across.

shots.vo: That account can't reach the controls he wants. So he reads through internal messages until he finds login details for someone with far more access.
shots.visual: Scrolling internal chat; a highlighted line glows.

shots.vo: Now Graham can change the email and password on almost any Twitter account in the world.
shots.visual: Twitter's admin tool on screen; a cursor hovers over 'change email'.

shots.vo: Phase two: make money. But Graham's name on the forum is mud. Nobody will buy from him.
shots.visual: A PHASE 2 card; a reputation meter at zero.

shots.vo: So he uses middlemen with good reputations: a 19-year-old in England and a 22-year-old in Orlando. Neither seems to know the full story.
shots.visual: Two avatar cards slide in: 'ENGLAND, 19' and 'ORLANDO, 22'.

shots.vo: Their forum ad offers any Twitter account for 2,500 to 3,000 dollars, paid in Bitcoin. Short, rare usernames sell fast.
shots.visual: A forum ad with a price tag; Bitcoin coins dropping.

shots.vo: Meanwhile, Twitter's security team is noticing strange calls and odd logins. Someone is inside. The clock is ticking.
shots.visual: Twitter's security room; red alerts on screens; staff gathering.

acts.name: Act 5: Phase Three, the Big Scam

shots.vo: Graham wants one last, bigger payday. Phase three: a crypto giveaway scam. Send Bitcoin, and you'll get double back.
shots.visual: A PHASE 3 card; a fake 'DOUBLE YOUR BITCOIN' banner.

shots.vo: 15 July 2020. The first scam tweets go out from crypto accounts and exchanges, one after another.
shots.visual: Tweet cards labelled with crypto company names pop up.

shots.vo: Then he goes big. Elon Musk's account posts it. Then Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos, Kanye West, MrBeast, Apple, Uber, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.
shots.visual: The wall of famous names; each card turns red with the same scam message.
shots.anim: Cards flip red faster and faster.

shots.vo: In total, 130 accounts are targeted, and scam tweets go out from 45 of them. Millions of people see them.
shots.visual: A counter: 130 targeted, 45 tweeted; a view counter racing.

shots.vo: Most people see through it. Some don't. Money starts landing in the Bitcoin wallet, and Twitter deletes the tweets as fast as it can.
shots.visual: A wallet meter filling; a bin swallowing tweets.

shots.vo: That evening, Twitter does something it has never done: it stops verified accounts from tweeting at all.
shots.visual: A giant plug yanked from the wall; blue ticks go grey.

shots.vo: It kicks every employee off the internal network, one session at a time. Graham is cut off. The hack is over.
shots.visual: Screens going dark row by row; the bedroom screen goes black.

shots.vo: The shutdown had side effects. News outlets went quiet, and a US weather service office couldn't tweet a tornado warning.
shots.visual: A weather map with a tornado symbol; a 'can't tweet' error.

shots.vo: Graham's take was reported at over 100,000 dollars. Crypto exchanges froze his wallets, which stopped even more money from reaching him.
shots.visual: A wallet with a padlock clamped on it.

shots.vo: It doesn't take long. The middlemen are traced through their forum accounts, emails and internet addresses.
shots.visual: Investigators linking a forum profile, an email and an IP address with string.

shots.vo: Two weeks after the hack, US prosecutors charge three people: the two middlemen, and a teenager they don't name.
shots.visual: A press podium; three charge sheets, one with a blacked-out name.
shots.anim: Sheets slap down; one name blacked out.

shots.vo: The teen's court hearing happens on a video call. It's hijacked by pranksters blasting music, and the judge has to stop it.
shots.visual: A video-call grid; a prank tile flashes; the judge's tile looks shocked.

shots.vo: In 2021 Graham pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three years in a juvenile facility, then three years of probation. Because he was 17, he avoided adult prison.
shots.visual: A gavel; '3 YEARS + 3 YEARS PROBATION'.

shots.vo: Another member, a British man named Joseph O'Connor, was later arrested in Spain and sentenced in the US to five years for a string of cybercrimes.
shots.visual: A Spain map pin; then a cell door.

shots.vo: The scary part is how simple it was. No brilliant code. Just a phone call and a fake web page.
shots.visual: The phone and the fake page side by side, glowing.

shots.vo: A 17-year-old briefly held the voices of presidents and billionaires. He used them to steal Bitcoin. It could have been much worse.
shots.visual: The red wall of accounts; a single phone in a teen's hand.
shots.anim: Wall dims; phone screen stays lit.

shots.vo: He wasn't the first teenager to break into giants. In part two: the boys who stole the next Xbox before Microsoft even released it.
shots.visual: A sealed game-console box with a 'STOLEN' tag.
End card.
shots.onscreen: THE KIDS WHO HACKED THE WORLD · PART 2 NEXT

hooks: A 17-year-old took over Obama's, Musk's and Bezos's Twitter in one afternoon. All he needed was a phone call.
In July 2020, Barack Obama's Twitter asked you to send him Bitcoin. A teenager in Florida was typing.

fixes: Twitter hack date 15 July 2020; 130 accounts targeted, tweets from 45 (Twitter's own figures).
Scam proceeds reported around $117,000-$120,000 in Bitcoin (source said 'up to $180,000'); kept as 'over $100,000'.
Greg Bennett SIM-swap: 2019 (source implied 2018); 164 BTC stolen. NYT linked it to an alias of Clark; he was not charged. Stated with care.
Clark pleaded guilty March 2021: 3 years juvenile facility + 3 years probation.
Charges announced 31 July 2020: Mason Sheppard (19, UK), Nima Fazeli (22, Orlando), and an unnamed juvenile. Middlemen named only by age and place in VO.

Joseph O'Connor: arrested in Spain July 2021, extradited, sentenced June 2023 to 5 years for several cybercrimes including Twitter-hack conspiracy (source said 'not for the Twitter hack'; corrected to neutral wording).
National Weather Service tornado-warning tweet issue kept, worded as 'a US weather service office'.
Methods described at high level only (phone call, fake login page); no technical how-to.
cuts: Archive interview and podcast clips cut.
Chat-log readouts with slurs and handles cut.
Everything rewritten in our own words.
